one_liner: Go framework for writing Redis-protocol servers; its 136-line map clone out-ran redis-server about 2x on a 2016 laptop pipeline test.
what_it_does: Redcon parses the Redis wire protocol (RESP and telnet-style inline commands) and hands each command to a Go callback, so you build your own server that redigo, redis-py, jedis and redis-cli can talk to. The API is ListenAndServe(addr, handler, accept, closed) plus Conn and Command types, with ListenAndServeTLS, unix-socket listeners, a ServeMux, a built-in PubSub (SUBSCRIBE/PSUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH) and Conn.Detach for taking over a connection. It is not a Redis replacement: every command, data structure and persistence rule is yours to write.
how_it_is_fast: Each connection gets its own goroutine that reads into a growable 4 KB buffer, parses every complete command in that buffer in one pass, runs the handler for each, appends all replies to one byte slice and flushes it with a single write per batch, so a 512-deep pipeline costs a handful of syscalls. With GOMAXPROCS above 1 the Go scheduler spreads connections across cores, which single-threaded Redis cannot do. In the benchmark the handler is a map lookup under a sync.RWMutex with no persistence, expiry or data-type machinery, so most of the gap is less work per command rather than a faster event loop; the README itself names no mechanism.
when_to_use: You need a custom service (spatial index, proxy, cache front, test double) that existing Redis clients can talk to without a new client library.
Your service is written in Go and you want the goroutine-per-connection model with plain blocking-style handlers.
Read-heavy, deeply pipelined traffic from many connections on a multicore box: the README's multi-threaded GET (3,993,610.25 rps) scales past the single-threaded run (2,403,846.25).
You want Redis-compatible pub/sub, TLS or unix-socket serving out of the box.
when_not_to_use: You actually need Redis: no persistence, expiry, replication, cluster or data types come with it; the benchmarked clone has SET, GET, SETNX, DEL, PING, QUIT, pub/sub and a blank CONFIG stub.
Facing untrusted clients without a length guard: the parser has no cap on multibulk count or bulk length, and crafted lengths can pin a core or crash the process (see gotchas).
Write-heavy multi-core workloads behind one global lock: the README's multi-threaded SET (1,944,390.38 rps) is slower than single-threaded (2,018,570.88).
A C++ codebase that wants an in-process library: this is Go and runs as a separate server or sidecar; the author's C port tidwall/redcon.c is the in-process option.
Tail-latency-bound services: the README publishes throughput only, no latency percentiles.

integration.dependencies: github.com/tidwall/btree v1.1.0, github.com/tidwall/match v1.1.1 (used by PubSub)
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.20 (go.mod since commit 7776fcd, 2026-07-22, which uses unsafe.String)
integration.platforms: any Go target with the net package (TCP, unix sockets, TLS)
integration.thread_safety: Handlers run concurrently, one goroutine per connection, so shared state needs your own locking (the example uses sync.RWMutex); a Conn is meant to be used inside its handler, and a detached connection must be flushed and closed by its new owner.

gotchas: The comparison is cross-run: the Redis row (SET 941,265.12, GET 1,189,909.50) was published on 2016-08-20 (commit 9e38e36) and never re-run, while the Redcon rows were re-measured twice, at SET 3,119,151.50 on 2016-09-07 (commit 4276409) and SET 2,018,570.88 after the 2016-09-18 API rewrite (commit 67c21aa). The 2.1x ratios pair runs a month apart on different code; the original same-day ratios were 1,320,655.00 vs 941,265.12 for SET (about 1.40x, derived) and 1,552,354.25 vs 1,189,909.50 for GET (about 1.30x, derived).

Parser robustness, found by reading redcon.go and resp.go at HEAD (not executed): readCommands has no upper bound on the multibulk count and its 'for j := 0; j < count; j++' loop keeps incrementing past the buffer without breaking, so '*1000000000000000000\r\n' spins the connection goroutine for about 1e18 iterations; a bulk length near MaxInt64 makes 'i+size+2' overflow negative and index the buffer out of range, an unrecovered panic that ends the process (redcon.go has no recover). The exported ReadNextCommand (used by evio's Redis example) checks 'count <= 0' instead of the bulk length n, so '$-2' passes and 'packet[i:i+n]' panics.

Stored arguments are sub-slices of a per-command copy of the whole raw RESP message, so keeping cmd.Args[2] in a map (as the clone does) retains the key and framing bytes too, and every command costs one allocation.

Over a real network the gap shrinks: in issue #3 (2016) the author's two-droplet test gave single-threaded Redcon 687,994.50 rps vs Redis 622,045.25 (about 1.1x, derived) at -P 128 -c 128; the benchmark clone's CONFIG stub reads cmd.Args[2] unchecked, so a two-argument CONFIG command panics it.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick redcon over evio when you want a simple goroutine-per-connection handler API with pub/sub, TLS and Detach and your connection count is moderate; evio (an epoll/kqueue event loop that reuses redcon's ReadNextCommand parser) only matched Redis at pipeline 1 in its own table. Neither replaces Redis; both are frameworks for your own RESP server.
verified_claims_summary: redis-benchmark (-t set,get -n 10000000 -P 512 -c 512, one fixed key, 3-byte values) against the example Go-map clone versus redis-server with AOF off (version not stated) on a 2.8 GHz Core i7 MacBook Pro with Go 1.7: single-threaded Redcon SET 2.02M vs 0.94M rps (about 2.1x) and GET 2.40M vs 1.19M (about 2.0x), but the Redis row is from a 2016-08-20 run and the Redcon rows from a 2016-09-18 re-run.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-07-22, a number-parsing fix), MIT, single-package Go module that is easy to vendor; the headline numbers are a 2016 first-party cross-run comparison (CLAUDE.md precedent sends cross-run comparisons to D), and the parser should get length limits before it faces untrusted clients.
